transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Reyes (Redwood SE), Janelle Park (BlueWave Head of ML Platform), Ravi Singh (BlueWave SRE), Liam O'Connor (BlueWave Product)
Shared artifacts: short GCS link to logs (redacted), benchmark spreadsheet: bit.ly/bluewave-poc-bench (note: redacted for PII)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Follow-up to reliability incident; discussion focused on 5xx spike, request timeouts, and rate limiting behavior. Action items assigned.

Transcript:
[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick roll call, we have Janelle, Ravi, Liam from BlueWave and Marcus and I from Redwood. How are you guys?
[00:14] Janelle Park: Doing good, thanks. Yep, we want to get to the bottom of last week's 5xx spike.
[00:22] Marcus Reyes: Cool. I'll start with a quick recap of what we saw on our side, and then we can go into customer logs.
[00:30] Marcus Reyes: So around 2026-05-01 14:20 UTC we observed a burst of traffic that correlated with elevated tail latency and a series of 5xx responses from the Redwood edge -- looks like a mix of timeouts and internal errors.
[00:45] Ravi Singh: Yeah that matches our side. We had a scheduled batch job that overlapped with peak user traffic, so ingress doubled for about 7 minutes. We did see a bump in the 429s earlier and then it cascaded to 5xxs.
[00:58] Ava Chen: Important to note, the model variant you were hitting was rdx-1.2-quant (the POC default) which has slightly different memory/KV characteristics than the full 1.2 fp16.
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: Could be that the quantized variant is more memory sensitive? We thought quantization would help with throughput but maybe it's causing evictions under sudden bursts.
[01:25] Marcus Reyes: Exactly, so one hypothesis: KV cache eviction + larger concurrency during the burst caused more cache misses and extra compute, leading to backend timeouts. Another hypothesis is that the ingress rate exceeded the configured autoscale ramp so requests sat in the queue longer and timed out.
[01:42] Janelle Park: On our side, we saw retries from the application side too — our client retries were aggressive. That probably exacerbated the load.
[01:55] Ravi Singh: Quick question: what are the default retry/backoff settings in your hosted API? Our team had set retry=3 with no jitter in the client lib.
[02:08] Marcus Reyes: Default guidance we've been giving is exponential backoff with jitter; the platform itself will retry some transient errors depending on the integration, but client-level retries without jitter can create thundering herd. We'll share a recommended snippet.
[02:25] Ava Chen: I'll tuck that under action items. Marcus, do you want to walk through the traces we pulled?
[02:30] Marcus Reyes: Sure. I have a sample request/response pair from the 14:22 UTC window — I'll paste the redacted snippet in the shared doc. What you'll see is elevated queue time (~450ms) before the request reaches the runtime and then a 504 from internal gateway in a subset of calls.
[02:48] Liam O'Connor: 450ms queue time — is that typical for spikes or is that abnormal?
[02:52] Marcus Reyes: For normal loads we aim for queue sub-100ms; 450ms is elevated and indicates we didn't have enough workers scaled up fast enough or the kernel selection path encountered a slow branch.
[03:05] Janelle Park: Is there an easy mitigation on our side? We can change client retries and add jitter immediately.
[03:12] Marcus Reyes: Yes, reduce retries and add exponential backoff with jitter. Also consider a circuit-breaker at the client so it stops hammering when 5xx rates climb.
[03:23] Ravi Singh: We can implement circuit breaker. Also curious about rate limits — we saw 429s. Can you confirm how soft limits vs hard limits behave for our POC account?
[03:35] Ava Chen: For POC accounts we have soft throttles that try to smooth traffic, but under sustained bursts we will return 429s. There's also a hard limit configured per-customer; we can review and if needed bump the soft threshold for your pilot window.
[03:50] Liam O'Connor: That'd help for the next test window.
[03:55] Marcus Reyes: Something else to consider: request size and context length. A few of the requests during the window were hitting 8k token contexts which increase memory pressure and may make quantized variant more likely to spike.
[04:12] Janelle Park: Noted — we'll audit the average prompt length. We do have approx 10% of calls that are long context.
[04:20] Ava Chen: Next let's go through a short timeline of the incident from the logs that BlueWave shared. Ravi, you sent us the ingress graphs?
[04:27] Ravi Singh: Yeah uploaded to the shared GCS. The big increase is at 14:18, peak at 14:22, tapering off by 14:30.
[04:36] Marcus Reyes: Thank you. From our side the spike coincides with a transient kernel fallback on some instances (we saw a few fall back to a slower execution path). Combined with high concurrency that's our likely proximate cause.
[04:50] Janelle Park: When you say kernel fallback, is that automatic? Can it be avoided?
[04:56] Marcus Reyes: It's automatic: the runtime may choose a different kernel based on runtime signals. We have mitigations — e.g., pin instances to a path or use a different model profile — but for hosted POCs we don't usually pin kernels. For Dedicated or Private deployments you can pin kernels and we can ensure more consistent behavior.
[05:12] Ava Chen: That's a good point — part of the POC goals should be to validate under expected burst patterns. We can simulate these in a scheduled benchmark.
[05:20] Liam O'Connor: What's the recommended load test pattern? Ramp vs step?
[05:23] Marcus Reyes: Ramp is better for autoscale, but you should include sudden step bursts to validate throttling and circuit-breakers. We'll provide a template in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:35] Janelle Park: On the topic of logs, can Redwood provide more detailed stack traces or only high-level status? We need to reproduce the machine behavior for our SRE postmortem.
[05:45] Ava Chen: We can provide filtered traces and markers (we will redact any PII). We'll include timestamps, request IDs, and high-level gateway error types.
[05:54] Ravi Singh: Sounds good — please exclude any user content.
[05:57] Ava Chen: Absolutely.
[06:02] [06:02] (crosstalk) 
[06:08] Marcus Reyes: Quick item — we noticed some client behavior where retries were immediate; that combination with the autoscaler ramp means you can overwhelm the queue. We'll attach a recommended backoff of initial 200ms, factor 2 exponential, jitter, and max 5s.
[06:27] Liam O'Connor: That should be straightforward.
[06:30] Janelle Park: Any thoughts about switching to a non-quantized model variant temporarily during the heavy window?
[06:36] Marcus Reyes: Yes switching to the fp16 variant will reduce kernel fallback risk at the expense of slightly higher GPU memory. For short burst windows that's often worth it. We can set an automated policy to route traffic to the fp16 variant when queue times exceed threshold.
[06:52] Ravi Singh: Is that something we can control via the API or is it an ops change?
[06:57] Marcus Reyes: For hosted accounts, Redwood ops can enable a routing policy for you; for Dedicated/Private you control it via config. We'll note this as an option.
[07:06] Ava Chen: Okay let's capture the immediate mitigations: 1) customer to reduce client retries + add jitter, 2) Redwood to share redacted logs and recommend backoff snippet, 3) consider temporary model variant switch during the next test.
[07:20] [07:20] (short pause)
[07:30] Liam O'Connor: We also want to understand the billing implications if we switch to fp16 variant for bursts.
[07:36] Ava Chen: There's a modest cost delta; we'll include approximate unit economics in the follow-up note. Marcus, can you approximate delta?
[07:43] Marcus Reyes: Rough ballpark: fp16 might be ~15-20% higher cost per token for these workloads depending on token mix, but it reduces error risk. We'll include a more precise estimate in the doc.
[07:56] Janelle Park: Good to know.
[07:58] Marcus Reyes: On telemetry — we recommend instrumenting two additional metrics: queue_time_95 and kernel_fallback_rate. Those will help trigger routing changes before 5xxs spike.
[08:12] Ravi Singh: We can add those to our dashboards.
[08:17] Ava Chen: Any legal/security blockers that would prevent you from sharing logs for analysis?
[08:22] Janelle Park: No, as long as PII is redacted. We have an NDA and SOC2 requirements; audit logs are fine.
[08:30] Ava Chen: Great. We'll ensure logs are redacted and shared through the secure bucket.
[08:36] Marcus Reyes: Next, a quick discussion about rate limiting behavior — you mentioned earlier you saw 429s, did those precede the 5xxs or come after?
[08:45] Ravi Singh: We saw an initial few 429s and then 5xxs started showing up as the system tried to keep up. So throttling didn't fully prevent downstream failure.
[08:56] Marcus Reyes: That pattern suggests retries created more backend pressure after initial throttling. So client-side throttling + backoff is key.
[09:06] Liam O'Connor: For our next scheduled test, can you temporarily raise the soft throttle so we can validate throughput?
[09:13] Ava Chen: Yes, for the POC window we can bump the soft threshold for a limited time if you want to do a controlled run; you'll need to confirm the exact window so we can monitor.
[09:22] Janelle Park: Let's plan for 2026-05-10 14:00 UTC for a controlled throughput run (subject to internal scheduling).
[09:30] Marcus Reyes: Noted. We'll provision extra monitoring and watch queue_time_95 and 5xx rate live.
[09:38] Ravi Singh: Great.
[09:41] [09:41] (short verbal ack)
[09:45] Ava Chen: Before we move to concrete configs, Marcus, could you summarize the open root-cause hypotheses?
[09:52] Marcus Reyes: Sure: 1) KV cache eviction and increased compute from cache misses on quantized variant; 2) Autoscaler ramp lag causing elevated queue times; 3) Aggressive client retries creating thundering herd; 4) Kernel fallback to slower path under memory pressure. We'll prioritize mitigation items in that order.
[10:12] Janelle Park: I like that ordering.
[10:16] Marcus Reyes: For mitigation we'll do: immediate client retry/backoff change, temporary soft-throttle bump for controlled test, provide redacted traces, run a dedicated load test including step bursts to replicate, and consider automatic routing to fp16 variant when queue_time_95 exceeds threshold.
[10:34] Liam O'Connor: For the load test, can Redwood provide the test harness or should we use our own tool?
[10:41] Marcus Reyes: We have a simple harness template in the benchmark spreadsheet; we can share a small k6 script and example config.
[10:49] Janelle Park: That would be helpful.
[10:52] Ava Chen: Okay, let's capture action items — I'll send a follow-up email with the logs link, recommended backoff snippet, k6 harness, and a cost delta estimate.
[11:03] Marcus Reyes: I'll also include a recommended circuit-breaker snippet and the kernel fallback notes.
[11:10] Ravi Singh: On our side we'll get the ingress charts and confirm the planned test time.
[11:17] Liam O'Connor: And we'll audit prompt lengths and try to eliminate long contexts where possible for the next run.
[11:25] Ava Chen: Any other questions or concerns?
[11:28] Janelle Park: Just one — if we do hit more 5xxs in the next run, what's the escalation path?
[11:34] Ava Chen: You can open a high priority support ticket and we will spin up an incident channel; Marcus will be on-call for this account during the test window.
[11:42] Marcus Reyes: Yep, and we'll also have ops watch the cluster logs.
[11:45] Janelle Park: Thanks everyone.
[11:48] Ava Chen: Alright, quick recap of next steps...
[11:52] (Recap)
[12:00] Ava Chen: 1) Redwood: share redacted logs and traces (Ava/Marcus) by 2026-05-07. 2) Redwood: share recommended retry/backoff + circuit-breaker snippet and k6 harness by 2026-05-09. 3) BlueWave: run audit of prompt lengths and confirm test window 2026-05-10 (owner: Janelle/Ravi). 4) Both: schedule follow-up deep-dive for 2026-05-11 to review test results.
[12:30] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good.
[12:33] Janelle Park: Thanks, appreciate the quick turnaround.
[12:36] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone; we'll follow up in email with links and notes.
[12:40] [End of recording]
